references.text: The Passover lamb was not to be left until morning, and whatever remained was to be burned with fire—the same principle applied to holy meat that must not be left over.
The manna was not to be kept until morning; it was holy food from God that had to be eaten within the appointed time.
The context of the ordination offering (millu'im) referred to in verse 34.
Rules for the thank offering: the meat had to be eaten on the same day or the next, and whatever remained on the third day was to be burned with fire.
The execution of the ordination ceremony where Moses commanded that whatever remained of the meat and bread should be burned with fire.
Peace offerings were to be eaten on the day of sacrifice or the following day, but what remained on the third day had to be burned—it was holy and must not be dishonored.
The thank offering had to be eaten on the same day; nothing was to be left over until morning.
Thematic parallel: Leviticus 7:15 confirms that the prohibition against leaving sacrificial food until morning is a general rule for certain holy offerings, not only for the ordination.
Highlights the consistent liturgical logic that fat and meat from festival offerings must not be left until the next morning.
Reinforces the principle by showing that the prohibition against leaving the offering until morning also applies specifically to the Passover festival offerings.
